sweep_summary: All seven title-works with stress in the title are Glottolog machine mis-assignments (title word 'rhetorical' matched to Kinaray-a [krj]); they concern German, Dutch, Hebrew and English question prosody and were not downloaded.org, Glottolog, the Dialectologia journal site and ScholarSpace. New open sources read: (1) Pefianco et al. 2016 Ortograpiya Kinaray-a (sec. 1.2, pp. 10-12) — a Kinaray-a-specific accent-mark inventory with penult/ultima stress crossed with final glottal and a four-way minimal set tobò/tobô/tobó/tobo: CONFIRMS the catalog's lexical coding, does not supersede Zorc 1977; (2) Rentillo 2025 Dialectologia 34 — says West Bisayan stress patterns are 'overwhelmingly similar' across Panay varieties, otherwise silent on placement; (3) Lobel 2013 dissertation — silent. Zorc 1967 primer (held by the project) also confirms lexical stress with a penult default. Not obtained: Limpiada 2015 'The Phonology of Kinaray-a as Spoken in Antique' (PNU thesis; HIGH priority — the only dedicated Kinaray-a phonology known, no copy or catalogue record found) and Tondares 2015 Taramdan sa Lantipulong Kinaray-a (print, medium). catalog's classification stands; deciding source remains Zorc 1977. All downloads.

new_statements.quote: Sa alpabeto nga Kinaray-a, may tatlo ka mga dagmit nga ginagamit (wara ti dagmit kon malagday): 1. Ang dagmit nga pasiput (´) 2. Ang dagmit nga palala (`) 3. Ang dagmit nga panguru (^) ... Ang Pasiput. Ang tinaga nga may dagmit nga pasiput, ginamitlang kang tayoyon nga may duun sa pinakaorihi nga kunla (syllable) ogaring wara ti pakuga nga tonog. Halimbawa: mará, likód, bukún, kokó, matá ... Ang Palala. Ang tinaga nga may dagmit nga palala, ginamitlang kang tayoyon nga may duun sa ikarwa antis ang pinakaorihi nga kunla kag nagatapos sa pakuga nga tonog ... Halimbawa: sahì, balità, batà, langkà
new_statements.translation: In the Kinaray-a alphabet three accent marks are used (no mark when [the word is] malagday, the plain/unmarked type): 1. the acute (pasiput ´) 2. the grave (palala `) 3. the circumflex (panguru ^) ... The acute: a word with the acute is pronounced with stress on the last syllable and without a glottal sound, e.g. mará, likód, bukún, kokó, matá ... The grave: a word with the grave is pronounced with stress on the second-from-last syllable and ends in a glottal sound, e.g. sahì, balità, batà, langkà. [p.12 adds: the marks are usually omitted in writing but may be used on homographs with different meanings, e.g. tobò 'growth', tobô 'of the same age', tobó 'sugar cane', tobo 'pipe'.]
new_statements.citation: Pefianco, Anna Cecilia R., Danny S. Tabuyan, Felicia M. Flores, Cornelio V. Ysulat Jr. & Ritchie D. Pagunsan (Dungug Kinaray-a Komisyon sa Polong Kinaray-a). 2016. Ortograpiya Kinaray-a. New York: Innobril. ISBN 978-1540619891.
new_statements.reading: The native-speaker language commission's orthography treats Kinaray-a word accent as lexically distinctive: stress may fall on the ultima or the penult, cross-classified with a final glottal stop, giving four-way minimal sets (tobò/tobô/tobó/tobo), with an unmarked default type ('malagday', parallel to Filipino malumay = penult, no glottal). This is a diacritic inventory rather than a phonological rule statement, but it is a first-hand, Kinaray-a-specific (not pan-Bisayan) confirmation that stress is contrastive between penult and ultima, i.e. the catalog's lexical coding.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's only stress statement for Kinaray-a (Pefianco et al. 2016 orthography, sec. 1.2) treats stress as lexically distinctive between penult and ultima. Zorc's 1968-73 field transcriptions, including the minimal pair tábuʔ/tabúʔ and same-shape words stressed on different syllables, are consistent with that lexical coding and are the earliest first-hand evidence for it; they add nothing on a rule, weight, or secondary stress, and they are raw elicitation data rather than a phonological statement.
new_statements.translation_language: Kinaray-a forms in Zorc's phonetic transcription with English glosses; the one heading is English
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated anywhere in the notes. Every transcribed word carries an acute accent on its stressed vowel (and a colon for a long penult vowel). Stress is written on the penult in some words (búgtuŋ, lámaŋ, sákup, búktut, bá:taʔ, ká:hoy) and on the ultima in others of the same syllable shape (tubús, sadáŋ, tanán, mayád, baláy, kagát), and the pair tábuʔ 'meet' vs tabúʔ 'happen' shows stress alone distinguishing two lexemes. The data therefore support penult-or-ultima stress that is lexically fixed and not predictable from syllable weight; Zorc does not say so in words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated. A grave accent appears in the struck-through 'hùnaʔhúnaʔ' 'think' (p. 45) and in 'maŋà' (p. 42, laundry story), which may mark a weaker accent on the first member of a reduplication or on a proclitic, but there is no comment.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The p. 45 page headed 'stress: balik' lists ten entries (sneeze, sound, spit, squeeze, think, wave, witch, ringworm, yawn) all struck through, i.e. forms whose stress was re-checked; the 'General intonation patterns' fields on both checklist information sheets (pp. 48, 57) are left blank; the Lambunao checklist (pp. 58-59, from a Peace Corps volunteer) is written without any accent marks.
new_statements.identity_note: The accented material is Antique Kinaray-a: the Proto-Austronesian and Proto-Philippine worksheets (pp. 2-28) name informant Sally de la Vega (secretary to Congressman Zaldivar; autobiography p. 40 gives birthplace Lanag, Hamtik, Antique, 1948) for Hamtik & San Jose, Antique; the 2 Oct 1968 Linguistic Checklist (pp. 47-55, site Bicol-Tiwi) names Sonny Pacificador, San Jose, Antique, born Naga City, mother tongue Kinaray-a (Bikol-speaking mother); the 2 Aug 1973 checklist (pp. 33-38) is unattributed. The second Linguistic Checklist (pp. 56-59, Iloilo City, June 1969) is Lambunao (Iloilo) Kinaray-a from Jim Jackman, a Peace Corps volunteer whose mother tongue is English, and carries no accent marks, so it says nothing about stress. Page 3 glosses 'big' as bahúl with a marginal '(dialect) háŋgüd'; p. 30 is a copy of the Kinaray-a Ave Maria from Carroll 1959:69 with accents added.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim on the page scan we hold of Zorc 1977 pp. 50, 216, 218, at the stated sections; Kinaray-a ('Kin') is explicitly named in the accent minimal pairs (ráhaq : raháq; bə́təŋ : bətə́ŋ) and in the closed-penult rule example (taqú- + -i → táwq-i). (2) The source is a 1977 comparative-historical monograph, but it is first-hand (Zorc's own Bisayan fieldwork) and is the standard reference on Bisayan accent; Glottolog 5.1 has no grammar or phonology of Kinaray-a at all (its 47 'descriptive' hits are computerized mis-assignments from the word 'rhetorical'), so there is no better-ranked description to displace it. (3) Everything open that I could download now -- Zorc 1967 primer, Zorc 1972 OL, Zorc 1978 PL C-61 (pp.71-75), Zorc 1979 handout, Zorc 1993 OLSP 24, and Zorc's 1972 Kinaray-a field notes on SEAlang -- either confirms (phonemic penult/ultima accent in Bisaya

sources.quote: p.20 Table 2: '(A) Phonemic length and shortness, as inherited from PPH (< PHN, PMP, PAN): Bisayan (except Kuyonon and Tausug), Coastal and Pandan Bikol, ... Tagalog.' and '(K) Accent is used inflectionally, that is morphemic accent: ... most Central Philippine languages.' p.19: 'In all Philippine languages stress or pitch accent is a syntactic (grammatical) feature ... it does not even necessarily coincide with length. ... Stress normally is a way of marking word boundaries and usually has a low functional load in words with a closed penult (CVC.CV(C)) ... Note Bisayan usually has CV́C.CV(C)'
sources.note: The author's later typological summary places 'Bisayan (except Kuyonon and Tausug)' in class A (inherited phonemic length) and notes the Bisayan closed-penult pattern; a compact second citation for the lexical + CVC-penult coding that currently rests on the 1977 monograph alone.

sources.citation: Rentillo, Philip. 2025. Lexicophonetic dialectology of Panay. Dialectologia 34: 235-271.
sources.quote: The group is also known to have minimal reflex variations which can be explained by the RDL and RGH Laws (Conant 1911, 1912), and a canonical three-vowel system /a, i, u/ with the exception of Kinaray-a varieties mainly in Antique featuring /ə/. Stress patterns are overwhelmingly similar especially among cognates. Deviances were noted as idiosyncratic features, and when verified with a reference sample informants would confirm that their initial utterance and the sample are both acceptable.
sources.locator: p.248 (sec. on West Bisayan phonological homogeneity); p.253 (North Antique 'accent')
sources.note: A lexicostatistic/phonetic dialect survey of Panay (Kinaray-a, Aklanon, Hiligaynon, Capiznon). Its only word-stress remark is that stress patterns are 'overwhelmingly similar' across West Bisayan varieties among cognates; the other 'accent' remarks (North Antique 'accent.. more similar to that in Pandan', 'fast, rough accent') are impressionistic dialect-accent labels, not placement rules. Silent on where stress falls. Its reference list gives no Kinaray-a phonology beyond Zorc 1972/1977 (no Limpiada).
